Sometimes life happens. Sometimes only one player manages to show up to a session. As a DM, what are some good tips/sessions/systems for when you want to entertain a party of one?

One tip is to become a party of two. You can play side-by-side using the Mythic Game Master Emulator, $6.95 or The Conjectural Roleplaying GM Emulator, pay what you want.

Both are system agnostic. You can use either with your favorite Science-Fiction game, Dungeons & Dragons, any old school game, even Vampire the masquerade. For the sake of the example,I'll assume you're doing Fantasy Dungeon Delving.

Both work similarly: in broad terms, there are multiple outcomes. Mythic has 4 outcomes, Exceptional Yes, Yes, No, and Exceptional No.

So put yourself in a place and ask a yes or no question. For example, "We're in a dungeon, do we see a door before us?". In Mythic, you roll percentile and use the table provided, which uses a chance for odds of something happening (it might be impossible, unlikely, 50/50, a sure thing, etc.) and then there's a chaos level applied. Chaos affects percentages, and as things get out of control, it increases. Roll dice and you have your answer. It's up to you to interpret the answer, so here are likely outcomes:

  • Exceptional Yes: There is a door and it's locked or guarded.

  • Yes: there is a door.

  • No: there is no door.

  • Exceptional No: There is no door, and now you can't find the entrance you came in. Perhaps you are trapped.

  • Note: you interpret how Exceptional Yes/No is handled. Another way of handling exceptional no could be "there is no door, and you can't see anything but the hall". As long as all who are playing are happy with the decisions made, there aren't bad or wrong answers.

Let's say you have a yes, you could next ask "is the door unlocked?" and roll. Or perhaps you just walk in and ask "is there a monster?" and ask. An exceptional yes might indicate a monster and a trap, for example.

Basically you set up a scene (we're in a dungeon), establish a thread (the goal, such as save the princess), and deal with randomness.

The Conjectural Roleplaying GM Emulator, is similar (you roll percentiles) and get multiple outcomes:

  • No, and unexpectedly

  • No, but

  • No, and

  • No

  • Yes

  • Yes, and

  • Yes, but

  • Yes, and unexpectedly

Instead of giving you odds and chaos levels, it has three tables: one for questions about knowledge, one for questions about conflict and one about endings. CRGE has you set a scene (like in a story or a book). So using a similar sense to the the situation above, you still have scenes and threads, and a surge count (cough Chaos Factor cough), and tables for the unexpected (which Mythic calls randomness). Again, you ask yes or no questions.

So you're in a dungeon and you ask, "Do we see a door?" Since this is about knowledge, you'd roll on that table. Asking about monsters would be about conflict.

  • No, and unexpectedly - No door, roll on unexpectedly table, which has 20 unexpected side effects of your question.

  • No, but - There is no door, but there is another way in (secret door, or maybe there's a doorway without a door).

  • No, and - there is no door, and maybe you're trapped from escaping the dungeon, etc.

  • No - There is no door.

  • Yes - There is a door.

  • Yes, and - there is a door, and guards in front of it? there is a door and it's locked. Remember, you're making this up as you go. There isn't a wrong answer as long as you both agree as to the outcome.

  • Yes, but - There is a door, but it's open. There is a door, but there are also two more doors down the hall, etc.

  • Yes, and unexpectedly - There is a door, and roll on the unexpected table.

Mythic - you pay for it, and you get 54 pages with many examples, and it's well detailed.

CRGE - pay what you want (which also means you can put a 0 in the amount, although $5 is the suggested price). It's only 32 pages. Has fewer details/examples, so there's less hand holding.

It does slow down things when you have to ask about evert detail (are there any lights? Do I hear anything at the door?), but you can speed either system up, by assuming every room is a pitch black hole, etc.

If you're playing First Edition AD&D, you've got a treasure type by monster (in the Monster Manual), so you can ask the yes/no question: does the monster have treasure? In 5E, there are random treasure tables in the DMG, so you could use the same question. Don't ask "is there copper?" - because you haven't stated how much, and then you'll be tempted to ask, "is there silver?", then "gold?", etc. Until you turn the dungeon into the Publisher's Clearinghouse Give-a-away.

Note these tables work just as well for any kind of adventure. So if you want a city adventure, you can ask are the people friendly? etc.

Edit: And in case you're wondering, this can work for larger than parties of two exactly the same way. You just go GMless.
